obs: "The new act took effect simultaneously with the repeal of the first act; its provisions may, therefore, more properly be said to be substituted in the place of, and to continue in force with modifications, the provisions of the original act, rather than to have abrogated and annulled them." ... "There was no moment in which the repealing act stood in force without being replaced by the corresponding provisions of the revised statutes. In practical operation and effect, therefore, they are rather to be considered as a continuance and modification of old laws than as ah abrogation of those old and the reenactment of new ones."
"except so far as they have been repealed or affected by subsequent laws"
Bear Lake & River Water Works & Irrigation Co. v. Garland

"Upon comparing the two acts of 1888 and 1890 together, it is seen that they both legislate upon the same subject, and in many cases the provisions of the two statutes are similar and almost identical."
Federal Intermediate Credit Bank of Columbia v. Mitchell
"The provisions of the Judicial Code are to be construed as continuations of existing statutes, and no change of intent is to be implied unless clearly made manifest."
United States v. United States Coin & Currency

"under Pa. Stat. Ann., Tit. 46, 582, if the repeal of a penal statute is accompanied by a re-enactment at the same time of the repealed laws provisions in substantially the same terms, a prosecution will be saved."
Countyof Oneida v. Oneida Indian Nation of NY

“Although there is a formal repeal of the old by the new statute, still there never has been a moment of time since the passage of the [old] act . . . when these similar provisions have not been in force. Notwithstanding, therefore, this formal repeal, it is . . . entirely correct to say that the new act should be construed as a continuation of the old . . . .”
"Although Revision Notes are not conclusive evidence of congressional intent"
